question: A 61-year-old woman comes to the physician for a follow-up examination 1 week after undergoing right-sided radical mastectomy and axillary lymph node dissection for breast cancer. She says that she has been unable to comb her hair with her right hand since the surgery. Physical examination shows shoulder asymmetry. She is unable to abduct her right arm above 90 degrees. When she pushes against a wall, there is protrusion of the medial aspect of the right scapula. Injury to which of the following nerves is the most likely cause of this patient's condition?

options.opa: Upper trunk of the brachial plexus

reasoning_chain: CHAIN: Axillary lymph node dissection -> potential nerve injury -> shoulder asymmetry -> 80% CHAIN: Inability to abduct right arm above 90 degrees -> possible nerve involvement -> scapular winging -> 70% CHAIN: Scapular winging on the right side -> likely long thoracic nerve injury -> inability to comb hair with right hand -> 80%
enhanced_information: The patient's symptoms of shoulder asymmetry, inability to abduct the right arm above 90 degrees, and scapular winging on the right side are indicative of a likely long thoracic nerve injury. This condition can lead to difficulty combing hair with the right hand. The most likely cause of this patient's condition is injury to the long thoracic nerve (opc). The evidence path confirming scapular winging as a result of long thoracic nerve injury supports this conclusion.
